group.passage:
In 1956, African honeybees were introduced into Brazil to improve honey production in the tropical climate of South America. However, they started to mix with European honeybees already living there and produced a new kind of “Africanized” honeybees that are better at setting up hives and at reproducing than European bees. Keeping Africanized bees poses a challenge to beekeepers. Generally, beekeepers keep their bees in [[1]] wooden boxes, or hives. After the worker bees fill a hive with honey, the beekeepers open the lid of the hive and blow a few puffs of thick, cool smoke into the hive to help calm the bees, [[2]] easier to collect the honey.
The problem with keeping Africanized bees is that they are more defensive than European bees. Even the slightest bump against the hive may [[3]] an alarm. A large quantity of smoke is needed to calm the bees. Two or three beekeepers may need to work together to safely harvest the honey. And they may need to wear heavier beekeeping suits even in hot, [[4]] weather. Beekeepers may also collect less honey from Africanized bee hives. European bees form search parties and work together to collect flower nectar from which honey is made, while Africanized bees usually work alone in search of flowers. Therefore, less nectar is brought back to Africanized bee hives. Africanized bees also spend less time storing honey but more time caring for young bees. That may be because they [[5]] in a tropical climate where not much honey is needed for food during the winter.

tags.topic: Africanized honeybees and the challenges of keeping them
